notes.meaning: David hears God ("the LORD") speak to someone David calls "my Lord." Jesus himself used this verse to show that the Messiah, God's promised King, is David's son and also David's Lord, so he is more than a man. Sitting at God's right hand means the highest honor and a share in God's rule. It is also a picture of rest after his work was done. A "footstool" pictures enemies fully beaten, like old kings who put their feet on the necks of defeated foes. God promises to do this in his own time.

other.label: Modern scholarship
other.view: Some scholars doubt that David wrote this psalm. They think Jesus was using the common belief of his day. They place the psalm later, among priest-kings of Israel after the exile.

notes.meaning: The "scepter" is the King's rod of power. Many teachers say it stands for the gospel, the good news about Jesus, carried by the power of the Holy Spirit. It went out from Zion, which is Jerusalem, where the preaching of the gospel began. Christ rules even while enemies still surround his people. His church stands firm and keeps growing in a world that opposes it.

The King's people come to him freely, like volunteers and not forced soldiers. They are also like freewill offerings, giving their whole selves to him. They wear "holy splendor," like priests' robes, which stands for holy lives. They are as many and as fresh as drops of morning dew. Most teachers say the "dew of your youth" means the many young believers who gather to Christ. Some say it means Christ's own lasting strength.

differ.view: God's grace works with special power in his people and makes them willing to come to Christ. So no believer can boast that they chose God by themselves.
The verse describes the free, generous character of Christ's people. It does not teach that grace forces people to come. God always treats people as free to choose.

other.label: Catholic and Orthodox
other.view: The old Greek and Latin Bibles read part of this verse as "from the womb, before the morning star, I have begotten you." Many early church teachers took this to mean the Son's birth from the Father before time began.

notes.meaning: God makes a promise with an oath and will never take it back. The King will also be a priest. A priest is someone who stands between God and people and offers sacrifice for sin. Melchizedek was both a king and a priest long before Aaron's family of priests began (Genesis 14). No ancestors or successors are listed for him. The book of Hebrews uses this verse to show that Jesus is our priest forever, greater than the old priests. He offered himself once for our sins, and he always lives to pray for us.

other.label: Modern scholarship
other.view: Some scholars link this verse to later Jewish rulers who were both priest and ruler. One of them, Simon, was called "high priest for ever" (1 Maccabees 14:41).

notes.meaning: Now the scene moves to battle. "The Lord" stands at the King's right hand to help and protect him. Some teachers say this is God the Father fighting beside Christ. Others say it is Christ himself. Either way, the King and God act as one. Even powerful kings who fight against him will fall. This happens on "the day of his wrath," the set time when God's patience with those who refuse him runs out.

The King will judge all nations fairly, not in blind anger. The picture of fields full of the dead is a battle scene. It shows that every power standing against him will be overthrown. Many teachers say it should be read spiritually, as the defeat of all evil. Crushing "the leaders" or "the head" may also echo God's first promise that the serpent's head would be crushed (Genesis 3:15).

Many read this as a warrior who stops only for a quick drink from a stream. Then he keeps chasing his enemies until he wins and can hold his head high. Many also see Christ's suffering here, as the bitter "brook" or cup he drank for us. After that came his rising from the dead and his glory. He humbled himself first, and so God lifted him up.
